title: 四十七店と手入れ  (Forty-Seven Stores and a Raid)

segments.t: At a loud celebration party, Toru Muranishi raises a glass to forty-seven store openings in three months and sets his sights on one hundred. Meanwhile, Takei raids a delivery van—where the old picture-book trick suddenly stops working—and Muranishi slips away to go home. Listen to the celebratory toasts and the sudden police raid.
おかげで三カ月で四十七店出店できた。
次は百店目指そう。乾杯！
よく見てくださいよ、刑事さん。
Celebration and danger collide here: Muranishi rallies his crew at the hall while Takei springs a trap at the warehouse. Let's hear the key lines.
おかげで三カ月で四十七店出店できた。

'Thanks to you all, we opened forty-seven stores in three months.' Starting with "okage de" gives warm credit—'thanks to your support'. "Sankagetsu" counts three months, "yonjuunana-ten" counts forty-seven shops, and "shutten dekita" says they managed to open them.
次は百店目指そう。乾杯！

'Next, let us aim for one hundred stores. Cheers!' "Tsugi wa" spotlights what comes next, and "mezasou" rallies everyone—'let's aim for'—around "hyakuten", a hundred shops. Then comes "kanpai", literally 'dry glass', the universal toast for 'cheers!'.
'Show me the cargo.' "Nimotsu" covers luggage, packages, or freight. "Misero" turns "miseru", to show, into a sharp police order with zero polite padding.
'They are all picture books.' Trying the old checkpoint excuse, the driver pairs "zenbu", all of them, with "ehon", picture books, plus reassuring "desu yo".
'Never mind that, bring them out.' Idiomatic "ii kara" brushes aside excuses—'enough already' or 'never mind that'—before "dase", the blunt command of "dasu", take out.
よく見てくださいよ、刑事さん。
'Take a good look, detective.' "Yoku" before "mite kudasai" means 'closely' or 'thoroughly', nudging Takei to spot the cash inside. "Keijisan" addresses a plainclothes investigator politely.
'Are we good to go now?' "Mou ii desu ka" literally asks 'is it good already?', a handy everyday check for 'are we done here?' or 'may I go now?'.
'Alright, arrest him.' Unlike local patrolmen, Takei pockets nothing: "yoshi" signals 'alright, got what we needed', and "taiho shiro" orders an immediate arrest.
'Here is a bonus for all of you!' Back at the party, rough plural "omaera", you guys, marks Muranishi's rowdy bond with his staff before borrowed English "boonasu da".

'I am going home.' Amid all the noise, one quiet word—"kaeru", to return home—says everything. Japanese needs no 'I' when the speaker's own next move is unmistakable. Now let's hear the whole party and warehouse raid sequence again straight through.
おかげで三カ月で四十七店出店できた。
次は百店目指そう。乾杯！
よく見てくださいよ、刑事さん。
From celebratory "kanpai" to quiet one-word "kaeru", you heard how Japanese can rally a crowd or slip out of a room in just a couple of syllables. See you soon.
